content_voiceover: This page covers AML pathogenesis genes and prognostic factors. Question twelve asks which mutated gene is most prevalent in cytogenetically normal AML, and the answer is NPM1. NPM1 mutations are found in about a third of all AML cases and are even more common in patients with a normal karyotype, often paired with FLT3 ITD mutations. Question thirteen asks which factors are unfavorable for outcome, and the answer combines GATA-1 expression together with adverse cytogenetics, specifically monosomy five or seven, deletion five q or seven q, exaggerated hyperdiploidy of more than forty seven chromosomes, trisomy eight, translocation between chromosomes six and nine, trisomy eleven, and complex karyotypes with multiple abnormalities. Notably, NPM1 mutation by itself, without FLT3 ITD, is actually a favorable marker, and early blast clearance during induction is a good prognostic sign, not an unfavorable one, which is why those two options were excluded from the correct answer.
keypoints: NPM1 is the most common mutation in cytogenetically normal AML
NPM1 mutation alone, without FLT3 ITD, predicts favorable prognosis
Unfavorable cytogenetics include monosomy 5 or 7, complex karyotype, and translocation six nine
Early blast clearance during induction predicts a good outcome, not a poor one
keypoint_voiceover: For boards, remember NPM1 is the single most common mutation in cytogenetically normal AML. On its own, without FLT3 ITD, NPM1 mutation actually predicts a favorable outcome. The unfavorable side includes monosomy five or seven, hyperdiploidy, trisomy eight, translocation between chromosomes six and nine, trisomy eleven, and complex karyotypes. And don't be fooled, early blast clearance during induction therapy is a good sign, not a bad one.
